panels.title: Predictions/s by served model
panels.description: Requests answered per second, split by which model served them. telecom_v4_rolling = the caller supplied a 10-reading history (rolling features used); telecom_v3 = no history yet, or the caller never sends one. A demo agent always starts on v3 and switches to v4 after its 10th reading -- v3-only forever means history is never reaching the API.

panels.title: /predict requests/s per pod
panels.description: Traffic per pod. Kubernetes' Service load-balances round-robin, so with N healthy pods each should carry roughly 1/N of total traffic. One pod flat at 0 while others show traffic usually means it failed readiness and was pulled from the Service, not that it is idle.

panels.title: /predict latency p95 per pod
panels.description: 95th-percentile time to answer one /predict call, per pod (inference + best-effort DB write). Normal is well under 200ms on this hardware. A sustained rise usually traces to the Feedback DB write p95 panel below -- PostgreSQL contention, not the model itself, is the usual cause.

panels.title: Error ratio (4xx / 5xx)
panels.description: Share of requests answered with an error. 4xx = the request itself was invalid (e.g. history not exactly 10 finite values) -- a caller-side problem, not a service failure. ANY sustained 5xx is a real server-side problem and should be investigated immediately; 0% is the expected steady state.

panels.title: Serving pods scraped
panels.description: How many serving pods Prometheus is currently able to reach. Should equal your replica count (kubectl get deploy anomaly-api -n ml-serving). Lower than that means a pod exists but Prometheus cannot scrape it -- check kubectl get pods and the Kubernetes API server connectivity.

panels.title: API uptime (currently-serving process, minutes)
panels.description: Minutes since the OLDEST currently-running pod started. Resets to 0 on every rollout or pod restart -- this is informational, not a health signal by itself. A value that keeps resetting every few minutes without you deploying anything indicates pods are crash-looping.

panels.title: Feedback DB write p95
panels.description: 95th-percentile time spent writing ONE prediction to PostgreSQL (a slice of total /predict latency, see the p95-per-pod panel). Typically a few ms to tens of ms. If this climbs, /predict latency climbs with it even though the model itself is unchanged.

panels.title: Anomalous machines over time
panels.description: How many of the 200 machines are CURRENTLY flagged anomalous (a Gauge, reflecting the latest verdict per machine -- not a running total). The synthetic generator injects anomalies at roughly a 5% base rate (README), so with the full fleet reporting, single digits to ~15 is ordinary background noise; a sustained spike well above that suggests a real correlated event worth checking in Root cause spotlight below.

targets.expr: count((api_currently_anomalous{job="anomaly-api-pods",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) == 1) or vector(0)

panels.title: Currently anomalous machines
panels.description: The actual list behind the count above: every machine whose most recent prediction was anomalous, right now, per the freshest pod that has reported on it.

targets.expr: (api_currently_anomalous{job="anomaly-api-pods",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))) == 1

panels.title: Classifier anomaly probability by machine (top 25)
panels.description: XGBoost's own P(anomaly) = 1 - P(normal) for each machine's most recent reading, 0-1, same scale whether v3 or v4 served it. The production decision threshold is 0.6 (chosen by ml-model/select_threshold.py on an independent validation set) -- values clustered just under 0.6 are 'nearly flagged' and worth watching. The served verdict also OR's in the IsolationForest safety net, so a machine can be anomalous here even with a low bar shown.

targets.expr: sort_desc(topk(25, (api_classifier_p_anomaly{job="anomaly-api-pods",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"})))))

panels.title: Fleet-wide average CPU
panels.description: Average of the raw CPU % each machine's most recent request actually reported (not a synthetic value -- literally what the API received). Purely descriptive of current fleet load; there is no fixed 'bad' threshold here since machine types have very different normal baselines (a database server idles hotter than a web server, by design of the synthetic generator).

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="cpu",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))))

panels.title: Fleet-wide average network
panels.description: Average of the raw network MB/s each machine's most recent request reported. Same caveat as CPU: descriptive only, no universal threshold, since normal ranges differ by machine type.

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="network",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))))

panels.title: Fleet-wide average load
panels.description: Average of the raw load-average value each machine's most recent request reported. Same caveat: descriptive, not a threshold -- a machine's OWN per-machine, per-time-window baseline (not this fleet-wide average) is what the model actually scores it against.

targets.expr: avg((api_input_metric{job="anomaly-api-pods",feature="load_avg",machine_type=~"$machine_type"} and on(pod, machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"} == on(machine) group_left() max by (machine) (api_machine_last_seen_timestamp_seconds{job="anomaly-api-pods"}))))

panels.title: Root cause spotlight (last 5 minutes)
panels.description: Machines the /root-cause endpoint identified as the LIKELY ORIGIN of a correlated failure (not just anomalous themselves) in the last 5 minutes. Structurally, only machines with real downstream dependents in dependency_graph.json can appear here -- in this project, that means routers. Empty is the normal state; a router appearing here means multiple dependent machines are anomalous at once and this is the one the graph points to as the cause.

panels.title: Root cause events over time
panels.description: The same signal as the spotlight above, over time, so a recurring root cause (the same machine repeatedly implicated) stands out from a one-off.

panels.title: Distinct anomalous machines (since pods started)
panels.description: How many DIFFERENT machines have been anomalous at least once since the current pods started (a Counter, so it only grows -- unlike the 'currently anomalous' panels above). Resets to 0 on every rollout. High relative to 200 over a long session is expected; a high value within minutes of startup would be unusual.

panels.title: Distinct root-cause machines (since pods started)
panels.description: Same idea as the panel to its left, but for root-cause incidents specifically: how many distinct machines have been identified as a likely root cause since the pods started.

panels.title: Host VM — CPU usage (real)
panels.description: Real CPU usage of the VM itself, not a machine in the simulated fleet. Sustained above ~90% is worth attention -- this VM also runs Jenkins, SonarQube, Minikube and every service at once, so high-but-brief spikes during a build or a training run are normal.

panels.title: Host VM — RAM available
panels.description: Real RAM still available on the VM. This project has hit genuine out-of-memory failures before (documented in the README's operational incidents) -- treat low single-digit GB as a real warning, not just a number.

panels.title: Host VM — Disk free (root)
panels.description: Real free disk space on the VM's root filesystem. This has genuinely caused a real incident before: Elasticsearch (inside SonarQube) went read-only and failed the Quality Gate when this dropped too low, fixed with docker image/builder prune. Below a few GB free is a real, previously-experienced risk on this exact VM, not a theoretical one.

panels.title: Host VM — Load average (1m)
panels.description: Real 1-minute load average of the VM. As a rule of thumb, sustained load above the VM's CPU core count means more work is queued than the machine can run concurrently.

panels.title: Kubernetes — pod status
panels.description: Ready (1) / Not Ready (0) for every pod in ml-serving. Any pod stuck at 0 for more than a minute or two after a rollout usually means its readiness probe (GET /health) is failing -- check kubectl logs on that pod.

panels.title: Kubernetes — pod restart counts
panels.description: How many times each pod's container has restarted since it was created. 0 is normal. A number that keeps climbing means the container is crashing and Kubernetes is restarting it -- check kubectl describe pod for the reason (often an unhandled exception or a failed liveness probe).

panels.title: Kubernetes — replicas (desired vs available)
panels.description: Desired = what the Deployment (or the HPA, if it has scaled) asks for; Available = how many are actually ready right now. The two lines should track each other closely; a persistent gap means new pods are being scheduled but failing to become ready.

panels.title: Kubernetes — HPA CPU utilization
panels.description: Average CPU utilization the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is measuring across the anomaly-api pods. When this crosses the HPA's configured target (see kubernetes/deployment.yaml or the hpa.yaml manifest), Kubernetes adds replicas automatically; below it, replicas may scale back down.
